chunks: From him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Hasan ibn Mahboub, from Abdul Rahman ibn Al-Hajjaj, from Al-Qasim ibn Abdul Rahman Al-Ansari, who said:
I heard Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'A man came to my father Ali ibn Al-Husayn (peace be upon him) and said to him, 'Inform me about the Words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic:
And those in whose wealth there is a known right. For the beggar and the deprived.

The man said, 'So if it is not from the Zakat nor from the charity, what is it?' He said, 'It is something which the man takes out from his wealth; if he wishes, he gives more, and if he wishes, he gives less, according to what he possesses.' The man said to him, 'And what should he do with it?' He said, 'He uses it to maintain kinship, to feed a guest, to carry a burden, or to help a brother for the sake of Allah, or to repel a calamity that befalls him.' The man said, 'Allah knows best where He places His messages.'

key_terms.الصَّدَقَةُ الْمَفْرُوضَةُ: The imposed charity (often referring to Zakat or Khums in this context)
key_terms.الْحَقُّ الْمَعْلُومُ: The known right (referring to voluntary charity)

ai.seo_question: What is the 'known right' in wealth mentioned in Surah Al-Ma'arij according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (AS) clarifies that the 'known right' (al-haqq al-ma'lum) in Surah Al-Ma'arij refers to voluntary charity (sadaqah) distinct from obligatory Zakat, emphasizing its discretionary nature regarding amount and timing. This interpretation highlights the Shia scholarly view that this verse mandates proactive social welfare through maintaining kinship (silat al-rahim), hosting guests, and supporting the needy, thereby linking spiritual obligation with tangible social responsibility.
